title: Prudence
hook: practical wisdom: the right thing, the right way, at the right time

segments.voice: Yesterday, caritas: love as behavior, patient and kind, the one Paul says never fails. Your line was love lasts. What deed did you do without announcing it? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

"The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going." That's Proverbs, and it could be pinned above every inbox. A text arrives: your package is on hold, tap here and pay a small fee. One person taps before finishing the sentence. Another reads it twice, checks where it came from, and waits. Neither is necessarily smarter. One just looked well to his going. Faith, hope and love were the virtues aimed at God. Today we begin the four that Christian teachers call the cardinal virtues, the ones for running an ordinary life. The first is prudence.

The four are named together in the Book of Wisdom, which Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include and King James printings place among the Apocrypha. Speaking of wisdom, it says: "for she teacheth temperance and prudence, justice and fortitude." Christian teachers took that list and built on it. Prudence comes first in their order, because it steers the others. It's practical wisdom: knowing the right thing, the right way to do it, and the right time. Not cleverness, and not caution for its own sake. A prudent person can be bold. Jesus sends his disciples out with a strange pairing: "be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves." Sharp-eyed and gentle at once. That's prudence. Ecclesiastes gives the timing part: there is "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." The same true words can heal at one moment and wound at another. Prudence notices which moment it is. And this closes a week, so look back at what it's steered. Do not steal: give it back. A truthful witness: speak truly. Do not covet: enough is enough. Then faith, trust. Hope, an anchor. Love, the one that lasts. Each of those needs prudence to land well. Knowing when to speak a hard truth, how to give something back without a scene, where a concrete act of love will actually help. The commandments and the virtues say what. Prudence asks how, and when.
screen: `A WEEK THAT NEEDED HOW AND WHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause before one decision. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one choice waiting for you today, large or small: a reply to send, a purchase, a conversation. Ask three plain questions. What is the right thing here? What's the right way to do it? And is now the right time? Don't force an answer. Let each question sit for a few breaths. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom, as the letter of James invites. The bell holds the time.
Prudence. Practical wisdom: the right thing, the right way, at the right time. The virtue Christian teachers place first, to steer the rest.
Your line: wise in the moment. Today, before you hit send or say the sharp thing, take one breath and ask: is this the time? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox teaching names prudence among the cardinal virtues; some Christians practice it by praying before decisions, seeking counsel and weighing the timing of what they say and do.
